summary: Explains how filters that follow RFC 1858 can still be fooled by a variant of the tiny fragment attack, and recommends a fix. The attack hides important header information by splitting packets into very small pieces.

eli5.summary: A guard checks the front of each package. A sneaky person cuts the package so tiny that the part the guard needs to see arrives later.

questions: how to protect against tiny fragment attack
what is the tiny fragment attack
why does rfc 1858 indirect method fail
subtitle: How a combination of tiny and overlapping fragments can get past RFC 1858 firewall filters, and how to stop it.

tldr.problem: RFC 1858's Indirect Method for filtering fragmented packets can be defeated by combining the Tiny Fragment Attack with the Overlapping Fragment Attack.
tldr.mechanism: The attacker sends three fragments: a legal first fragment to an allowed port, a second 8-byte fragment at offset 0 that overwrites the destination port, and a third completing the message. None has a fragment offset of 1.
tldr.outcome: The fix is to also drop TCP fragments with offset 0 that hold less than a complete header, in addition to dropping those with offset 1.

today: RFC 3128 is Informational and updates RFC 1858. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem with the Indirect Method
sections.content:
RFC 1858 describes attacks on Internet firewalls that use packet fragments. Its Indirect Method (section 3.2.2) is vulnerable to a combination of the Tiny Fragment Attack and the Overlapping Fragment Attack.

The attack matters where filtering rules allow incoming connections to a machine while other ports on the same host are meant to allow only outgoing connections. Only the initial connection message needs to be fragmented; once the connection is established, further traffic is legal.
sections.eli5: An old rule for catching sneaky cut-up packages has a hole, and this memo explains it.

sections.title: The Attack in Three Fragments
sections.content:
Fragment 1 has offset 0 and length of at least 16. It holds a whole, legal header, typically a SYN to an allowed port such as 25 (SMTP). Fragment 2 also has offset 0 but length 8: only the ports and sequence number. It replaces the destination port with one that may not receive incoming connections. Fragment 3 has offset of at least 2 and completes the message; it is not part of the attack itself but is needed so the message is not passed up early.

In the RFC's example rules, fragment 2 aimed at Telnet (port 23) looks like part of an existing FTP data channel, so it passes. Depending on how the target reassembles, fragment 2 may overwrite fragment 1 and make a new Telnet connection.
sections.eli5: The first piece looks fine. The second piece quietly replaces the address on it.

sections.title: Why the Indirect Method Fails
sections.content:
The Indirect Method tries to stop both attacks solely by rejecting packets with fragment offset (FO) of 1. None of the attack fragments has FO=1, so none is rejected.

RFC 1858 assumes that forcing header fields out of the zero-offset fragment requires an FO=1 fragment. That holds for genuine fragments from bona fide software, but a forger is not forced to send FO=1 just by sending an 8-byte FO=0 fragment. The vulnerability flows from this false premise.
sections.eli5: The old rule assumed cutters always leave a certain piece. A forger does not have to.

sections.title: Countermeasures
sections.content:
As well as blocking FO=1 packets, it is also necessary to block FO=0 packets that hold less than a complete header. The RFC gives two rules:

if FO=0 and PROTOCOL=TCP and TRANSPORTLEN < tmin then DROP PACKET
if FO=1 and PROTOCOL=TCP then DROP PACKET

The Security Considerations section says the memo is concerned entirely with the security implications of filtering fragmented IP packets.
sections.eli5: Throw away any first piece that is too small to show the whole label, as well as the old rule's targets.

references.text: Ziemba, G., Reed, D. and P. Traina, "Security Considerations for IP Fragment Filtering", RFC 1858, October 1995.
